opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition is a bit counterintuitive at first. If what you ultimately care about is a small model, why spend all that compute training something huge you're never going to deploy? But the way I think about it is that the large model is basically a much better compressor of the data. It can extract structure from the training distribution that a small model trained from scratch on the same tokens just can't find on its own, because it doesn't have the capacity to explore that space efficiently.

Once you have that teacher, it gives you something much richer than the original labels. With hard labels or next-token targets, you get one bit of "this is the right answer." With distillation, you get the full distribution over outputs, all the "dark knowledge" about which wrong answers are almost right and how confident the model should be. That's a much denser training signal per example, so the student learns faster and generalizes better than it would from raw data alone.

The other piece, which a lot of my work has focused on, is on-policy distillation. In standard distillation the student imitates the teacher on the teacher's own outputs or on fixed data, but at inference time the student generates its own sequences and drifts into states it never saw during training. That's the classic exposure-bias problem. If you instead let the student generate and have the teacher give feedback on those student-generated sequences, you're training on the distribution the student will actually face. That closes a lot of the gap, and it makes the teacher even more valuable, since you can query it on whatever the student produces.

So the economics work out. You pay the cost of the big model once, and you can amortize it across many small models for different deployment settings: phones, latency-sensitive serving, whatever. Inference is where most of the compute goes at scale, so a better small model pays for the teacher pretty quickly. That's why basically every strong small model family now is distilled from something bigger. It's just the most compute-efficient path to a good small model that we know of right now.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a larger teacher can extract structure and provide a richer training signal that helps produce a better small model, making the teacher’s training cost worthwhile through distillation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is: the thing you actually care about is the quality of the small model, and the question is just what's the most compute-efficient path to get there. And it turns out that training a small model directly on the raw data is often not the most efficient path.

If you look at the scaling law picture, a small model trained to convergence on a fixed data budget hits a ceiling that's set by its own capacity to extract signal from the data. The pretraining loss, next-token prediction on web text, is a pretty noisy objective. A lot of the gradient signal is going toward modeling things that are essentially unpredictable, the randomness in human text, and the small model has to spend capacity figuring out which parts are learnable and which parts aren't.

A larger teacher basically does that work for you. Once you have a big model, its output distribution is a much cleaner target. Instead of a one-hot token, you get a full distribution that says, here are the plausible continuations and roughly how plausible each one is. That's dramatically more information per token. So when you distill, the small model is learning from a denoised version of the data, and it can get to a given quality level with far fewer tokens than it would need from scratch.

And the thing people sometimes miss is that the compute for the teacher is amortized. You train the big model once, and then you can distill it into a whole family of small models at different sizes, for different deployment targets. So if you're a lab that's going to ship several models anyway, the marginal cost of the teacher is spread out, and each student ends up better than what you'd get training it independently.

There's also a more subtle point around what you can do once you have a teacher. You're not limited to just matching logits on the original data. You can do on-policy distillation, where the student generates its own samples and the teacher scores them, which fixes the train-inference mismatch you get with standard supervised distillation. You can have the teacher generate synthetic data for domains that are underrepresented. You can use it to filter or rank. So the teacher becomes this general-purpose source of supervision that's much richer than static data.

So the short version is: big models are better at learning from data, and small models are better at learning from big models. Training the teacher is a way of converting compute into a higher-quality training signal, and that signal is reusable.

r001.rationale: The response says training a small model directly on raw data is often less compute-efficient, while a larger teacher provides a higher-quality, reusable signal that can produce a better small model.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that a larger model can be a much more compute-efficient way to learn a good representation, even if what you ultimately want to deploy is a small model. The larger model has more capacity, so it can discover patterns that the small model might struggle to learn directly from the raw data. Then you can transfer some of that knowledge through distillation.

The teacher also gives you a richer learning signal. Instead of just saying, “This is the correct next token,” it gives you a distribution over possible tokens, which tells the student something about which alternatives are plausible.

So you have to look at the total cost: training the teacher, distilling it, and then serving the student. If you’re going to run that small model a huge number of times, or reuse the teacher to train several students, the upfront investment can make a lot of sense.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger model can learn a good representation more efficiently even when the intended deployed model is small, then transfer that knowledge through distillation.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that a larger model can learn things that are hard for a small model to discover directly from the training data. Once it has learned those things, we can use it as a teacher to make the small model’s learning problem easier.

For example, instead of giving the student only a correct answer, the teacher can provide a richer signal about which answers are plausible, or generate demonstrations of how to solve a problem. So you’re separating discovering a useful behavior from learning to reproduce it. Those don’t necessarily require the same amount of capacity.

And the economics can make sense because you pay for the larger teacher during training, but you get to deploy the smaller student many times. If you care about inference cost and latency, spending more up front to get a better small model can be a worthwhile tradeoff.

r001.rationale: It explains that a larger teacher can learn useful behaviors and make the student’s learning easier, making the upfront training cost worthwhile for a good, cheaper small model.
